title: Little segregation in Englewood; first noticing it on the way to Boston
summary: Asked about Englewood's mix, Stewart says he noticed no segregation at home but first saw it on the train and in Boston stations and restaurants.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: What was the -- I was talking with Sonny Greer. He grew up in Long Branch, New Jersey.

And he told me that -- that one of the things was that he said in Long Branch there was like -- there wasn't any like segregation in an overt sense like a white and a black school. He said there was a certain -- there were certain kinds of racial restrictions, but by and large he more or less, you know, he and everybody else kind of -- everybody was kind of -- it was kind of a mixed neighborhood. So how was - what kind of neighborhood was yours?
Yeah, that's right, come to think of it.

That's about the way it was around home in Englewood. There wasn't really any segregation. What I mean, I didn't notice it, and especially at that age I was just like all of the fellows, you know, and girls in school. You know what I mean.
I played a little bit of basketball and what have you -- and we were just all like one another, you know.

When did you become aware of the fact that there was any social differences in terms of the treatment of people, Negroes as opposed to whites? Did you become aware of that in Englewood or after you left home?
I became aware of that more or less when I left home.

When I went to Boston, yes. Then at the -- a few things that happened, you know, even that I hadn't read about, you know, or heard about segregation and what have you, and that's when I started to see some of those things happen, you know.
Even at that time when I went to Boston by train, and even at that time. I noticed some things on the train going up even

Like the color of the parlor cars and what -- they had little restrictions, you know. Even the restroom facilities, what have you -- at times I did notice that they did have a place for colored, a place for white, you know, that, and, of course, even when I went to Boston restaurants
and railroad stations, you know, they had a bit of segregation there at that point.
